messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Graphic Designer
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 74

He is 33, European, divorced, and works as a graphic designer, a job that once felt like a good fit for the part of him that likes order, color, and control. Before the trauma, he describes himself as someone who could stay late at his desk without noticing the time, absorbed in layering images until they felt right. He was married then, living a life that felt predictable enough to be safe.

That changed during a police incident that he still struggles to tell in a straight line. He had been out late when he was stopped by police and what began as a routine encounter quickly escalated into something frightening and disorienting. He remembers the sharpness of commands, the sudden physical force, the sensation that the world had narrowed to flashing lights, hard voices, and his own body going rigid. He says that in the moment he did not understand what was happening; he only knew that he was scared and that no explanation seemed to matter. The experience left him humiliated and terrified, with the lingering sense that authority could turn instantly into danger. Even now, he feels his chest tighten when he tries to describe the night, as if his body begins reliving it before his mind can organize the memory.

In the weeks that followed, he tried to carry on as if nothing had changed. He returned to work and sat in front of design software, but he noticed that his attention kept slipping. He would stare at a blank screen and lose track of what he was supposed to do. Colors that once felt energizing began to seem harsh. He started checking doors and windows more often, especially at night. On the street, he found himself watching police cars before he noticed anything else. If he heard sirens, his stomach would drop. He says the sound does something immediate to him; his body reacts before he has time to think. He goes cold, scans for exits, and feels an urge to get away, even when he knows there is no present threat.

Sleep became difficult. At first he had trouble falling asleep because his mind kept returning to the encounter in fragments: a voice, a hand, the sound of his own breathing. Later, he began waking from vivid dreams in which he was again surrounded by officers and unable to make himself understood. After these nightmares, he would sit at the edge of the bed, listening for movement in the hallway, too alert to settle back down. He became irritable with his ex-wife, who at the time did not understand why he seemed distant and easily startled. Small comments could provoke anger, though he felt ashamed of how quickly he snapped. He began withdrawing from friends, turning down invitations and staying home more often, saying he was tired when in fact he felt unsafe around people and exhausted from staying on guard.

Over time, the strain on his marriage deepened. He describes becoming less present, less affectionate, and increasingly difficult to live with. He tried not to burden his wife with what he was feeling, but the silence grew between them. He felt misunderstood and, at times, judged for not “getting over it.” The divorce still sits heavily with him. He links part of the loss to the trauma, saying he was not the same person after that night and could not find his way back to the version of himself she had married. He carries guilt about that, along with a persistent sense of damage.

At present, he continues to work as a graphic designer, though he functions unevenly. Deadlines can still be met, but he often works in bursts, losing concentration when he is reminded of the incident or when he feels watched. He prefers remote work when possible, where he can control his environment and avoid unexpected interruptions. He has learned to map out routes in advance and chooses times to go out when the streets are quiet. He still becomes visibly tense around uniforms, officers, or even public safety announcements. He describes feeling as if part of him is always bracing for the next confrontation.

He is aware that the event has changed his relationship to safety, trust, and his own body. He does not speak about it with many people, partly because the memory is painful and partly because he worries others will not understand why it remains so present. In session, he often pauses before answering, as though he is deciding how much of the experience he can bear to put into words. Even then, the fear seems close to the surface, carried in the way he watches the door, the way he startles at sudden sounds, and the way his face tightens when the subject turns to police.
